title: Mastering the Rubenstein Defense | French Defense Strategic Guide | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: We open e4 and face a French — e6.
We play d4, taking the full center.
Black plays d5 and we answer the Tarrasch knight to d2.
Black captures on e4 — the Rubinstein French.
We recapture on e4.
Black plays a knight to d7 — the Rubinstein, incredibly solid and hard to break down. The classical setup with a bishop to d3 promises little, so I'll play one of the more enterprising modern lines.
We start with a knight to f3, the entry point to all of this.
This is the tabia — almost everyone plays a knight to f3.
We capture on f6.
Black recaptures. From this tabia White has five or six setups — a bishop to d3 is classical but the least promising.

I'll play c3 — a move with a very good reputation among top GMs. It looks purely positional, reinforcing the pawn, but a big point is that a queen check on a4 is a major idea while the king sits on e8: White develops on the a4-e8 diagonal and pressures Black before he completes development.
Black plays c5. The main moves for us are a knight to e5 or a bishop to e3.

A bishop to e3 — a developing move that pressures c5 and threatens to win a pawn with a capture on c5. If Black takes on d4 we recapture with the bishop, and the structure resembles an Alapin Sicilian, where a bishop in the center can be very powerful.

Black plays a knight to d5. A capture on c5 now runs into a knight capture on e3: even with queens off, Black recaptures the pawn and leaves us a poor structure plus the bishop pair — so the c5 capture is out. And a bishop check on b5 is ineffective, since Black just plays a bishop to d7.

So this is the moment for a knight to e5 — centralizing, and preparing a bishop check on b5 and a queen check on a4, against which a bishop to d7 no longer works: we take on d7, and the bishop to b5 wins the queen.

Black plays a6, preventing a bishop to b5 and taking the sting out of a queen check on a4. Our options: a capture on c5, though Black gets away with a knight capture on e3; or just a normal move like a bishop to d3, since a knight capture on e3 doesn't scare us — d4 stays secured and after castling we hit f7 while the d3 bishop eyes h7.
I'm leaning toward capturing on c5 — an interesting endgame if Black takes on c3.
In a classical game my intuition says try the capture on c5, posing Black the dilemma of whether to take on e3.

We've played the capture on c5. Its point: it opens the d4 square as a parking spot for the bishop, securing the knight and eyeing g7 — and any time Black plays f6, there's the queen-h5, g6, knight-takes-g6 trick, so we're never worried about being pushed off e5.
Black captures on e3.
We trade queens on d8.

Black recaptures and we take on e3 — and concretely we threaten a knight capture on f7, which is why this whole thing works: Black has to waste a tempo shuffling the king back to defend it. Our e3 pawn is weak but Black lacks the firepower to attack it, and we're not just keeping the extra pawn — we're playing to keep Black's bishops passive with b4.
Black plays a king to e8.
We play b4, building the pawn chain to keep the dark-squared bishop at bay. Now, optimal squares: e5 is a good temporary spot for the knight, but a knight to c4 heads for the b6 outpost.
Black plays a bishop to e7, aiming for a bishop to f6 — a threat we must address.
We start with a knight to c4 — removing the knight from e5 so a bishop to f6 won't come with tempo, and we'd play this move anyway.
Starting with the knight to c4 keeps our options flexible and discourages a bishop to f6, since a knight to c6 would come in with tempo.

Black plays a bishop to f6. This c5-b4-c3 construction is superb at winding down Black's queenside counterplay. I'll hold off a knight check on d6 — keeping the knight on c4 keeps its options open, like potential versus kinetic energy.
We play a king to d2 to secure c3 — the typical advice is not to tie a heavy piece to a menial task, so a rook to c1 would waste it; the king belongs on c2, defending c3 and off the d-file.
Black plays a king to e7. A rook check on d8 isn't scary, since we shift the king to c2 — what we really watch is how Black develops the c8 bishop.
So a bishop to e2, to meet a bishop to d7 with a bishop to f3 and beat Black to the long diagonal — these endgames hinge on who reaches a square first.
The king slides to c2. Against a bishop to d7 and a threatened check on a4, a prophylactic a4 stops the bishop reaching b5 and a4, and if a bishop to c6, we play a bishop to f3, disarming it.
Black plays a bishop to d7. His bishop on f6 is a terrible piece — it only stares at a well-defended pawn — a lesson in understanding what a piece actually does.
We play a4 as planned — it stops the bishop's checks and lets us later push b5 and advance our majority.
A bishop to f3, disarming Black's light-squared bishop. We've disarmed both bishops; now the final stage is converting the extra pawn.
When you're holding your opponent's pieces back like this, be careful not to accidentally give up a square.
We recapture on f3.
A rook to d1 to contest the d-file — Black's last source of activity.
I'm not rushing the knight to d6 or b6 — on c4 it controls everything.
The point of the rook to d1 isn't so much to trade rooks as to contest the d-file; control it and we focus entirely on converting our four-on-two kingside majority.
Black plays g6 — paralyzed and low on time, reduced to waiting moves.
The key is not to hurry — a king to b3, bringing the king toward c4 and a future b5.
A rook to d6 — a classic idea, occupying the file to prepare doubling.
There's no other sensible square on the d-file, so we put the rook to d6.

After a trade on d6 we recapture with the knight — a pawn recapture only gives a temporary check, whereas keeping the structure paralyzes the knight against c3's weakness... no, we want the knight, keeping the pawns as they are.
The rooks trade on d6.
We recapture with the knight, pressuring the clock.
Black plays a rook to c7.
We bring the other rook to d1 — the whole point of our approach, controlling the d-file.
I'll play h3 to restrict Black's pawns and stop any g4 activity — there's no hurry.
A knight to e4, to freeze Black's kingside pawns so I can convert my majority without worrying about a Black passer.
Black plays f6.
Black's only long-term counterplay is a passed pawn via f5 and g4, so freezing his kingside pawns with the knight lets me convert my majority in peace.
A king to c4 — slightly risky, opening a rook trade, but the rook trade is winning. If Black plays a rook to d7...
Black plays a rook to d7 — pushing the b-pawn only helps us; b5 should win.
After the rook trade, a tactic wins another pawn.
f4 — knocking the bishop off e5, then a capture on f6 with check, and coming around to take on h5.
Black's bishop drops back to e5 to dominate the knight.
We extricate the knight by maneuvering the king to e4 to dislodge the bishop — the winning idea.
We take on h5.
Black threatens a king to g6. Do we rush the king to e4, or do we have a tempo to fix the queenside?
We play c4 first — an extra tempo — and only after a king to g6 do we play king to e4.
Black plays a king to g6.
We play king to e4. The magic: after a nasty bishop to c3 attacking b4, a knight to f4 comes with check.
The knight to f4 with check extricates the knight, and we win.
We play b5 — too many passers; we could even sacrifice the knight, but no need.
Black plays a bishop to b4.
We play c6 to create an outside passer on a6.
Black captures on c6.
We take on a6 — a passed pawn should be as far from the enemy pieces as possible.
Corner pawns are the hardest to stop — a knight to d3, and the rest is obvious.
A bishop to a7 — we head for c6 to dislodge it and push a7.

A knight to e5, the final nail — a knight to c6 and a7 are coming. That's how we convert. The Rubinstein French is named for Akiba Rubinstein, but it was actually first played in 1861 by Ignatz Kolisch, one of the top opening experts of the 1860s.
